title: What Refrigerant Does My Air Conditioner Use?
h1: Which Gas Is Used in an HVAC System? Refrigerants and Furnace Fuel Explained
description: Most home AC systems use R-410A, older ones R-22, and newer ones R-454B or R-32. Learn how to check your refrigerant type and what a low charge really means.
quick_answer: Most home air conditioners and heat pumps use R-410A. Systems from before about 2010 often use R-22, which is no longer produced. New equipment is moving to R-454B or R-32. You can find your type on the label on the outdoor unit. A gas furnace, by contrast, burns natural gas or propane for heat.
body:
"Gas" in an HVAC system can mean two different things. Your air conditioner or heat pump uses a refrigerant that moves heat from inside to outside. A gas furnace burns natural gas, or sometimes propane, to make heat. They don't mix and they do completely different jobs.

What does refrigerant actually do?

Refrigerant moves heat. Inside, it flows through the evaporator coil, picks up heat from your home's air and turns from a liquid to a vapor. The compressor outside squeezes that vapor, and the outdoor coil releases the heat outdoors. The refrigerant then cycles back inside to do it again.

A heat pump uses the same process in reverse during winter, pulling heat from outdoor air and bringing it inside. That works well in our mild coastal winters and on most inland nights.

Which refrigerants are common in home systems?

RefrigerantWhere you'll find itWhat to know
R-22Older systems, mostly installed before about 2010Phased out and no longer produced. Remaining supply is limited, so repairs cost more over time.
R-410AMost systems installed from about 2010 until recentlyStill widely in use and serviceable. New equipment is moving away from it.
R-454B and R-32Newer air conditioners and heat pumpsLower global warming potential. Installers need training and parts made for these refrigerants.

The refrigerant type affects repair options and cost, so it's worth knowing which one you have before something breaks. Refrigerants are not interchangeable. You can't top off an R-22 system with R-410A, and newer refrigerants need equipment designed for them.

How do I find out which refrigerant my AC uses?

Go to the outdoor unit and look for the metal or sticker data plate, usually on a side panel. It lists the model number, serial number and the refrigerant type, along with the factory charge. You might see "R-22," "R-410A," "R-454B" or "R-32."

If the label is faded, the model number can tell a technician what's inside. You can also check your installation paperwork. As a rough guide, if your outdoor unit was installed before about 2010, there's a fair chance it uses R-22.

Does refrigerant run out?

No. Refrigerant runs in a sealed loop and isn't used up the way fuel is. If your system is low, it has a leak. Adding refrigerant without finding the leak only buys time, and the system will lose it again.

Signs your system may be low on refrigerant:

  • Air from the vents isn't as cool as it used to be
  • The AC runs much longer to reach the set temperature
  • Ice forms on the indoor coil or the larger copper line outside
  • A hissing or bubbling sound near the lines or coil
  • Higher electric bills with no change in use

Handling refrigerant requires EPA certification and special tools. This isn't a DIY repair. Releasing refrigerant is illegal, and the pressures involved can cause injuries.

What gas does a furnace use?

Most furnaces in San Diego and Orange County run on natural gas from the utility. A few homes use propane, and some use electric heat instead, such as a heat pump or electric heat strips. A gas furnace burns fuel in a sealed chamber and vents the exhaust outdoors through a flue.

If you ever smell gas, a rotten-egg odor, leave the house right away. Don't flip switches or use the thermostat. Once you're outside, call your gas utility. If a carbon monoxide alarm goes off, get everyone out and call 911.

Should I repair or replace an R-22 system?

For a small fix on an R-22 system that isn't leaking, repair can still make sense. For a major leak or a failed compressor, replacement is often the more practical path because R-22 supply keeps shrinking and these systems are aging.

Our air conditioning technicians can tell you which refrigerant you have, check for leaks and walk you through your options with a free estimate.
faqs: Can I add refrigerant to my AC myself?

No. Handling refrigerant requires EPA certification, gauges and recovery equipment. A low charge also means there's a leak that needs to be found and fixed, so adding more without a repair just wastes money.
Can an R-22 system be converted to R-410A?

Not by simply swapping refrigerant. R-410A runs at much higher pressures and needs a compatible compressor, coil and oil. In practice, moving from R-22 means replacing the outdoor unit and usually the indoor coil.

New equipment is moving to lower-impact refrigerants like R-454B and R-32. Existing R-410A systems can still be serviced and repaired, so you don't need to replace a working R-410A system because of the change.

In normal operation it's sealed inside the system and isn't a concern. Leaking refrigerant can displace oxygen in a small closed space and can cause frostbite on contact. Leave leaks and repairs to a certified technician.
